name: Introduction to Data Analytics Tools and Techniques
objectives: Given something you care about at home, work or in your community, write one clear question that data can answer and list the data you need, starting with which, how many or how much
Using Google Sheets or Excel for the web, create a spreadsheet with clear headings and enter clean data, one heading per column in row 1 and one record per row, at least ten rows
Given a spreadsheet of data, sort a column from largest to smallest and filter to show only some rows, then clear the filter so all rows come back
Given a column of numbers, calculate a total with SUM and an average with AVERAGE, using the right range so both update when a number changes
Given your data and a free AI assistant, create a chart with a clear title and ask AI to explain a formula or error, choosing the right chart type and pasting no private data
When your sheet is finished, write two plain sentences that answer your question, check your work and share it safely, with a number that backs up the answer and sharing only with people who need it

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What data analytics is, and asking a good question
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write one clear question that data can answer.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you care about at home, work or in your community, you will write one clear question that data can answer and list the data you need, starting with which, how many or how much.
Data is information you can count or list: dates, amounts, names of places, number of visitors. Analytics means looking at that data to answer a question.
Every good project starts with a clear question. "Which day of the week does our food pantry get the most visitors?" is clear. "Tell me about the pantry" is not.
A clear question tells you what data to collect. To find the busiest day, you need the date and the number of visitors for each day.
Step by step:
- Pick something you care about: family, work, school or community.
- Write one question that starts with which, how many or how much.
- List the data you need to answer it.
Words to know:
- Data: information you can count or list, like dates, amounts or names.
- Analytics: looking at data to answer a question.
Try it now: Write one clear question about your family, work, school or community that numbers could answer. Under it, list the two or three kinds of data you would need.
You can now write a clear question and name the data needed to answer it.

options: Information you can count or list
Only numbers on a bank statement
check.why: Data is information like dates, amounts, places and visitor counts.

check.q: Your church wants to know if more people come in winter. What data do you need?
options: The date and number of people at each service
check.why: A clear question tells you to collect the date and the count for each service.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening a free spreadsheet and entering data
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a spreadsheet with clear column headings and your data.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets or Excel for the web, you will create a spreadsheet with clear headings and enter clean data, one heading per column in row 1 and one record per row, at least ten rows.
A spreadsheet is a grid of boxes called cells. Columns go up and down and have letters (A, B, C). Rows go across and have numbers (1, 2, 3). Cell B2 is in column B, row 2.
Free choices: Google Sheets at sheets.google.com with a free Google account, or Excel for the web at office.com with a free Microsoft account. Both work in a web browser and as phone apps.
Keep data clean: one heading per column in row 1 (like Date, Day, Visitors), one row for each record, and numbers typed as plain numbers with no extra words. Clean data makes every later step easier.
Step by step:
- Open sheets.google.com or office.com and start a blank spreadsheet.
- Give the file a clear name.
- Type a heading in each column of row 1.
- Enter one record per row below the headings.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a grid of rows and columns for working with numbers and lists.
- Cell: one box in a spreadsheet, named by its column letter and row number, like B2.
- Heading: the label at the top of a column.
Try it now: Open a free spreadsheet. Make three headings for your question (for example Date, Day, Visitors) and enter at least ten rows of real or practice data.
You can now start a free spreadsheet and enter clean data under clear headings.

check.q: In a spreadsheet, what are rows named with?
check.why: Rows go across and have numbers; columns have letters.

check.q: You typed "about 40 people" in the Visitors column. What do you change?
options: Type just 40 as a plain number
check.why: Clean data uses plain numbers so the spreadsheet can do math with them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Sorting and filtering
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort your data from largest to smallest and filter it to show only some rows.
This lesson builds toward: Given a spreadsheet of data, you will sort a column from largest to smallest and filter to show only some rows, then clear the filter so all rows come back.
Sorting puts rows in order, such as largest to smallest. Sorting the Visitors column from largest to smallest puts the busiest day at the top.
Filtering hides the rows you do not need right now. You could filter the Day column to show only Saturdays. Filtering does not delete anything; you can turn it off and all rows come back.
In both Google Sheets and Excel for the web, sort and filter are in the Data menu or on the Data tab. If you cannot find them, ask a free AI assistant: "How do I sort a column from largest to smallest in Google Sheets?"
Step by step:
- Click any cell in your data.
- Open the Data menu or Data tab and turn on a filter.
- Use the small arrow on a heading to sort largest to smallest.
- Use the arrow on another heading to show only some values, then clear the filter.
Words to know:
- Sort: put rows in order, like largest to smallest or A to Z.
- Filter: show only the rows that match what you choose, without deleting the others.
Try it now: Sort your main number column from largest to smallest and write down the top row. Then filter to show only one kind of row, and clear the filter.
You can now sort and filter a spreadsheet to find what you are looking for.

options: Puts rows in order, like largest to smallest
Deletes rows you do not need
check.why: Sorting puts rows in an order, such as the largest number first.

check.q: You only want to see the rows for Mondays. What do you use?
options: A filter on the Day column
check.why: A filter hides the rows you do not need without deleting them.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Formulas: SUM and AVERAGE
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use SUM to total a column and AVERAGE to find its average.
This lesson builds toward: Given a column of numbers, you will calculate a total with SUM and an average with AVERAGE, using the right range so both update when a number changes.
A formula is a small instruction that does math for you. Every formula starts with an equals sign (=).
=SUM(C2:C31) adds every number from cell C2 to cell C31. =AVERAGE(C2:C31) finds the average of those numbers. C2:C31 is called a range: all the cells from C2 down to C31.
If you change a number in the column, the total and the average update on their own. That is the power of a spreadsheet: no recounting by hand.
Step by step:
- Click an empty cell under your number column.
- Type =SUM( then the first cell, a colon, and the last cell, then ).
- Press Enter to see the total.
- In another empty cell, do the same with =AVERAGE( ... ).
Words to know:
- Formula: an instruction that starts with = and does math in a spreadsheet.
- Range: a group of cells, written like C2:C31.
- Average: the total divided by how many numbers there are.
Try it now: Under your number column, add a total with =SUM and an average with =AVERAGE. Change one number and watch both update.
You can now total and average a column with SUM and AVERAGE.

check.q: What is a range like B2:B20?
options: All the cells from B2 down to B20
check.why: A range is every cell from the first to the last, joined by a colon.

check.q: You want the total of spending in D2 to D15. What do you type?
check.why: =SUM(D2:D15) adds every number from D2 to D15.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a chart, with AI as your helper
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple chart and use AI to explain a formula or fix an error.
This lesson builds toward: Given your data and a free AI assistant, you will create a chart with a clear title and ask AI to explain a formula or error, choosing the right chart type and pasting no private data.
A chart turns numbers into a picture. A bar chart compares amounts, like visitors per day. A line chart shows change over time. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, like spending by category.
To make one, select your headings and data, then insert a chart from the Insert menu or Insert tab. Change the title to say what the chart shows.
A free AI assistant can explain formulas and errors. Type the formula or error and ask: "Explain this in simple words and how to fix it." Do not paste private data like names, addresses or account numbers; describe the columns instead.
Step by step:
- Select the headings and the data you want to show.
- Open the Insert menu or Insert tab and choose Chart.
- Pick bar, line or pie.
- Give the chart a clear title.
Words to know:
- Bar chart: a chart that compares amounts with bars.
- Line chart: a chart that shows change over time.
- Pie chart: a circle that shows parts of a whole.
Try it now: Make a bar or line chart of your data and give it a clear title. Then ask an AI assistant to explain what =AVERAGE(C2:C31) does in simple words.
You can now make a chart and use AI to understand formulas without sharing private data.

check.q: Which chart compares amounts, like visitors per day?
check.why: A bar chart compares amounts side by side.

check.q: Your formula shows an error and the sheet has clients' names. What do you paste into AI?
options: The formula and a description of the columns
check.why: Describe the columns and paste the formula, not private data.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Telling what the data shows
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write two plain sentences that answer your question and share the sheet safely.
This lesson builds toward: When your sheet is finished, you will write two plain sentences that answer your question, check your work and share it safely, with a number that backs up the answer and sharing only with people who need it.
Your work is not finished until someone understands it. Write two sentences: one with the answer, one with a number that backs it up. For example: "Saturday is our busiest day. We averaged 64 visitors on Saturdays, compared with 38 on other days."
Check your work before you share. Look for typos in numbers, blank rows and totals that look too big or too small. If something looks wrong, it probably is.
To share, use the Share button and choose who can see it. For data about people, share only with those who need it, and remove names or phone numbers if they are not needed.
Step by step:
- Write one sentence with the answer to your question.
- Write one sentence with a number that supports it.
- Check for typos, blank rows and odd totals.
- Share only with the people who need it.
Words to know:
- Finding: what the data shows, said in plain words.
Try it now: Final task: finish your spreadsheet with sorting, a filter, SUM, AVERAGE and a chart. Write two plain sentences that answer your question, check your work, and share it with one person.
You can now turn data into a clear, checked finding and share it safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clean data Missing headings, mixed words and numbers, or fewer than ten rows. One heading per column, one record per row, plain numbers for a month of data. The file has a clear name and the data needs no fixing. Sort and filter Data not sorted or filtered. Main number column sorted largest to smallest, and a filter used and cleared. Can say what the sort and filter showed. SUM and AVERAGE Formulas missing or using the wrong range. Correct SUM and AVERAGE on the number column. Shows that both update when a number is changed. Chart No chart, or the wrong type and no title. A chart of the right type with a clear title. The chart makes the answer to the question easy to see. Two-sentence finding No answer, or no number to back it up. One sentence with the answer and one with a supporting number. The work was checked and shared only with people who need it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What two parts does a good finding have?
options: An answer and a number that backs it up
A name and a phone number
check.why: One sentence gives the answer and one gives a number that supports it.

check.q: Your average visitors per day shows 4,200, but the pantry is small. What do you do?
options: Check for typos, blank rows and the formula range
check.why: A number that looks wrong probably is, so you check your work first.
